# HTTP Semantics
## [Copyright Notice](#rfc.copyrightnotice)

+ [1.1.](#rfc.section.1.1) [Purpose](#purpose)

Likewise, servers do not need to be aware of each client's purpose: a request can be considered in isolation rather than being associated with a specific type of client or a predetermined sequence of application steps.
This allows general-purpose implementations to be used effectively in many different contexts, reduces interaction complexity, and enables independent evolution over time.
HTTP is also designed for use as an intermediation protocol, wherein proxies and gateways can translate non-HTTP information systems into a more generic interface.
HTTP has been the primary information transfer protocol for the World Wide Web since its introduction in 1990.
It began as a trivial mechanism for low-latency requests, with a single method (GET) to request transfer of a presumed hypertext document identified by a given pathname.
As the Web grew, HTTP was extended to enclose requests and responses within messages, transfer arbitrary data formats using MIME-like media types, and route requests through intermediaries.
This specification uses the Augmented Backus-Naur Form (ABNF) notation of [[RFC5234]](#RFC5234), extended with the notation for case-sensitivity in strings defined in [[RFC7405]](#RFC7405).

It also uses a list extension, defined in [Section 5.6.1](#abnf.extension "Lists (#rule ABNF Extension)"), that allows for compact definition of comma-separated lists using a "#" operator (similar to how the "\*" operator indicates repetition). [Appendix A](#collected.abnf "Collected ABNF") shows the collected grammar with all list operators expanded to standard ABNF notation.
As a convention, ABNF rule names prefixed with "obs-" denote obsolete grammar rules that appear for historical reasons.
## [3.](#rfc.section.3) [Terminology and Core Concepts](#terminology)
HTTP was created for the World Wide Web (WWW) architecture and has evolved over time to support the scalability needs of a worldwide hypertext system.
Much of that architecture is reflected in the terminology used to define HTTP.

For example, though the URI of a resource might imply semantics that are not safe, a client can expect the resource to avoid actions that are unsafe when processing a request with a safe method (see [Section 9.2.1](#safe.methods "Safe Methods")).

HTTP relies upon the Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) standard [[URI]](#URI) to indicate the target resource ([Section 7.1](#target.resource "Determining the Target Resource")) and relationships between resources.
### [3.2.](#rfc.section.3.2) [Representations](#representations)

An algorithm, usually based on [content negotiation](#content.negotiation) ([Section 12](#content.negotiation "Content Negotiation")), would be used to select one of those representations as being most applicable to a given request.

This selected representation provides the data and metadata for evaluating conditional requests ([Section 13](#conditional.requests "Conditional Requests")) and constructing the content for [200 (OK)](#status.200), [206 (Partial Content)](#status.206), and [304 (Not Modified)](#status.304) responses to GET ([Section 9.3.1](#GET "GET")).
### [3.3.](#rfc.section.3.3) [Connections, Clients, and Servers](#connections)
As a result, a server *MUST NOT* assume that two requests on the same connection are from the same user agent unless the connection is secured and specific to that agent.
Some non-standard HTTP extensions (e.g., [[RFC4559]](#RFC4559)) have been known to violate this requirement, resulting in security and interoperability problems.
### [3.4.](#rfc.section.3.4) [Messages](#messages)
The term user agent refers to any of the various client programs that initiate a request.
The most familiar form of user agent is the general-purpose Web browser, but that's only a small percentage of implementations.

Other common user agents include spiders (web-traversing robots), command-line tools, billboard screens, household appliances, scales, light bulbs, firmware update scripts, mobile apps, and communication devices in a multitude of shapes and sizes.

Common origin servers also include home automation units, configurable networking components, office machines, autonomous robots, news feeds, traffic cameras, real-time ad selectors, and video-on-demand platforms.
Most HTTP communication consists of a retrieval request (GET) for a representation of some resource identified by a URI.
In the simplest case, this might be accomplished via a single bidirectional connection (===) between the user agent (UA) and the origin server (O).
### [3.9.](#rfc.section.3.9) [Example Message Exchange](#example)
The following example illustrates a typical HTTP/1.1 message exchange for a GET request ([Section 9.3.1](#GET "GET")) on the URI "http://www.example.com/hello.txt":
Client request:
GET /hello.txt HTTP/1.1 User-Agent: curl/7.64.1 Host: www.example.com Accept-Language: en, mi
Unless otherwise indicated, URI references are parsed relative to the target URI ([Section 7.1](#target.resource "Determining the Target Resource")).
It is *RECOMMENDED* that all senders and recipients support, at a minimum, URIs with lengths of 8000 octets in protocol elements.
Note that this implies some structures and on-wire representations (for example, the request line in HTTP/1.1) will necessarily be larger in some cases.
Two origins are distinct if they differ in scheme, host, or port.

Even when it can be verified that the same entity controls two distinct origins, the two namespaces under those origins are distinct unless explicitly aliased by a server authoritative for that origin.
Origin is also used within HTML and related Web protocols, beyond the scope of this document, as described in [[RFC6454]](#RFC6454).

In HTTP/1.0, a separate TCP [connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connection-oriented_communication "Connection-oriented communication") to the same server is made for every resource request.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP#cite_note-rfc1945-3):§1.3

In HTTP/1.1, instead a TCP connection can be reused to make multiple resource requests (i.e. of HTML pages, frames, images, [scripts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Client-side_scripting "Client-side scripting"), [stylesheets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cascading_Style_Sheets "Cascading Style Sheets"), etc.).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP#cite_note-rfc9112-4):§9.1,9.3 HTTP/1.1 communications therefore experience less [latency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_latency "Network latency") as the establishment of TCP connections presents considerable overhead, especially under high traffic conditions.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP#cite_note-5)
Enhancements added with HTTP/2 allow for less latency and, in most cases, higher speeds than HTTP/1.1 communications.
HTTP/1.0 added headers to manage resources cached by a client in order to allow conditional GET requests.
* A server must return the entire content of the requested resource only if its last modified time is not known by the client or if it changed since the last full response to a GET request.
* Header `Content-Encoding` was added to specify whether the returned content is [compressed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP_compression "HTTP compression").
The realm value string, if present, is combined with the canonical root URI to form the protection space component of the challenge.
This in effect allows the server to define separate authentication scopes under one root URI.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP#cite_note-:0-1)

A request identifies a method (sometimes informally called _verb_) to classify the desired action to be performed on a resource.

However, the HTTP/1.1 specification[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP#cite_note-rfc2616-36):§9 added five new methods: PUT, DELETE, CONNECT, OPTIONS, and TRACE.

As of 2022, HTTP/0.9 support has not been officially, completely deprecated and is still present in many web servers and browsers (for server responses only), even if usually disabled.

pages.title: HTTP GET Requests and Message Bodies: Standards, Changes, and Concerns
passages: Get app
Share
Any such body would be ignored by the server because there were “no defined semantics” for it .
This design made sense because GET’s purpose is to retrieve a resource by URL and query parameters, not to submit data (unlike POST).
Traditionally, clients and servers adhered to this rule: GET requests were sent without a payload, and any parameters were passed in the URL (query string) or headers.
**Evolving Specifications: Are GET Bodies Allowed?**
More recently, the HTTP core specifications were consolidated and updated again in **RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics, 2022)**.

* **RFC 7231 (HTTP/1.1 Semantics, 2014)** — Clarified that sending a payload with GET is not forbidden by syntax, but has _“no defined semantics”_ . The RFC warns that some implementations might reject such requests. This was a shift to accommodate edge cases without endorsing the practice. (Notably, RFC 7231’s publication officially obsoleted RFC 2616 , so it replaced the earlier rules with this updated guidance.)

* **RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics, 2022)** — Reiterated and strengthened the caution. It explicitly notes that content in a GET request _“cannot alter the meaning or target of the request”_ and might lead implementations to reject the request as a malformed or malicious one . It introduces security concerns (like request smuggling) and says clients **SHOULD NOT** send a body in GET unless they have prior knowledge the server expects it . This emphasizes that, even in 2022, the official stance is that GET bodies are not part of mainstream, interoperable HTTP usage.
These RFC references show a clear consensus: **the standards bodies acknowledge GET request bodies only to warn against using them**.
Even though newer specs don’t outright ban GET bodies, there are multiple reasons why using them is problematic:

* **Interoperability and Implementation Support:** Many HTTP client libraries, servers, and intermediaries still assume GET has no body. Some frameworks will actively prevent or alter such requests. For example, Salesforce’s platform (Apex) will convert a GET request with a body into a POST behind the scenes as a security measure . Web browsers’ Fetch API disallows bodies on GET/HEAD requests for compliance and security. If you attempt to send a GET with a payload, you may find the client or some proxy along the way drops the body, converts the method, or blocks the request as malformed.

* **Caching and Proxy Behavior:** HTTP caching infrastructure is built around the idea that GET (and HEAD) requests are cacheable and identified by their URI (and certain headers). Proxies and caches **ignore request bodies** when deciding if a response can be served from cache, since the body is not supposed to matter for GET. This means if you send different bodies on the same URI, a cache might treat them all as the same request — a recipe for confusion. One HTTP expert noted that no existing caching proxies support varying the cache key by an “arbitrary request body” for GET . Thus, a GET with a body could lead to cache misses or worse, cache **collisions** (serving the wrong content) because the cache doesn’t consider the body. This violates the expectation of GET being cache-friendly and could produce inconsistent behavior across clients.

* **Server & Security Concerns:** Some servers might handle a GET body in unexpected ways. A robust server would ignore the body for a GET, but a poorly implemented one might try to read it and run into errors or resource usage issues. Security appliances (like WAFs — Web Application Firewalls) often flag GET requests with bodies as suspicious. They may block them thinking it’s an anomaly or an attempt to bypass filters. In fact, a GET with a body can be exploited in certain **HTTP request smuggling** scenarios (where differences in how proxies vs. back-end servers interpret message bodies can be abused). The RFC 9110 explicitly warns of the potential for request smuggling if GET/HEAD bodies are sent through intermediaries that don’t expect them . Additionally, if a server mistakenly attempts to process a GET body, it could lead to instability. One Stack Overflow discussion noted a _“bugged Web server”_ might buffer the unexpected body indefinitely or mishandle it, leading to excessive memory use or even injecting that data into unrelated responses . This kind of unforeseen behavior underscores the risk — since GET bodies are so unusual, they’re less tested and could expose odd bugs.

* **Lack of Tooling and Standards for Use Cases:** If an application designer finds themselves needing to send a payload to the server to filter or shape the returned data, the standard approach is to use a different HTTP method (like POST) or to include parameters in the URL (query string). Because GET with body isn’t standard, many tools don’t offer first-class support for it. For example, some HTTP client libraries will throw an error if you try to add a body to a GET request. Many server frameworks will ignore the body by default. There has even been an attempt to introduce a new method (often discussed as **SEARCH** or **QUERY**) to handle “safe requests with a request body” for use cases like complex searches. The existence of such proposals is an acknowledgment that overloading GET with a body is not the right solution, and a different method would be clearer and safer. As of now, that proposal isn’t an official standard, so the pragmatic choice is to avoid GET bodies in favor of well-supported patterns.
**Conclusion**
The consensus in the engineering community is that while you **can** send a body with GET, you probably **shouldn’t**.
Doing so yields no benefits under the HTTP spec and invites numerous problems with caches, intermediaries, libraries, and servers.

If you need to send data to the server (e.g. submitting form data or performing a search with complex criteria), it is better to use an appropriate method like POST or define a new safe method, rather than relying on a GET request body.
